gearboxIsTheTier: THE RACE 7-SPEED'S DEFAULT RATIOS ARE NOT A PROPERTY OF THE CAR.
Identical at every gear AND at the final drive, on two cars sharing
nothing else: 2022 RWD coupe vs 2023 FWD hatch, 571 lb apart, 3 points of
front distribution apart. This is case G7, the gate on G4, and it opens the
gate: measuring SPREAD for 4/5/6/8/9/10 gears is worth doing, because one
It also means SPREAD[7] can simply be replaced with the measured set rather
than left as a fallback nobody trusts.
THE CONFOUND, STATED BEFORE ANYONE ELSE FINDS IT: both cars are
AWD-SWAPPED. 'The race 7-speed has fixed ratios' and 'the AWD swap installs
a standard gearbox' both explain this equally well. Nothing here separates
them. A third race 7-speed on a car that was NOT drivetrain-swapped costs
one screenshot and settles it — take that before acting on this.
crossCarConstants: MOST OF THE GAME'S DEFAULT TUNE IS A TEMPLATE, NOT A CALCULATION.
Identical on both cars, to every digit:
gearing      all seven ratios and the final drive
Different on the two cars — and every one of them is load-bearing:
The split is clean: anything that depends on the car's mass, its
distribution or its bodywork varies, and everything else is a constant the
game stamps on. Two cars is not a law, but it is a sharp enough pattern
that a third car disagreeing would be the interesting result.
casterIsFive: Case S7, second confirmation. The game's default caster is 5.0 on both
cars. The app prints 6.5 for the road family (moved there 2026-08-01 from
6.7 on ForzaTune's 5.5-6.5 band); the forums say 7.0.
This does NOT make 5.0 correct — a default is where the game starts you,
not where it is fastest, and every other default here is beatable. What it
does is remove the possibility that 5.0 was a one-car quirk. S7 still needs
the sweep against a panel figure to say which value is actually better.
dampingRatioConfirmed: The app builds bump as 0.63 x rebound, carried over from FH4/FH5 community
practice and sitting at tier 3 in CLAUDE.md as never FH6-confirmed.
The game's own default tune uses 0.62-0.63 at both ends of both cars. That
is four independent instances agreeing with the convention to within a
hundredth. Corroboration of the RATIO only — it says nothing about whether
the app's absolute damping numbers are right, which is still D-class work.
mbModelDoesNotTransfer: As predicted, and worth recording as a prediction that held rather than a
surprise. The GR86's coefficients applied to the Civic's default tune:
Out by 0.025, which is well outside the +/-0.005 rounding window, so this
is a real miss and not a two-decimal artefact. CLAUDE.md said the three
coefficients are that car's tires, geometry and unsprung mass and do not
The DIRECTION does transfer, which is the part that matters. The Civic runs
a stiffer front at both bar and spring (30.90 vs 21.50, 703.0 vs 596.6) and
reads BELOW 0.5 — exactly what a rear-share model requires. One point, so
it is consistent with the form rather than evidence for it. The three rows
aeroBodyTermAgain: Weak but same-signed. The Civic makes MORE front downforce than rear (361
vs 336) and still reads 0.50 rather than above it, so the rear body term is
against the GR86's b - a = 40. Both rear-biased, same order of magnitude.
But a single 2-dp readout constrains only the DIFFERENCE, not a or b, and
0.50 covers everything in [0.495, 0.505] — so b-a is really 'about 25, give
or take 7'. Do not treat this as a measurement of anything. A3's floor and
ceiling rows are what pin a and b.

rows.purpose: DIRECTION AND OFFSET — equal bars. The GR86 read 0.51 here, not 0.50, and the axle constants are why
SAME-RATIO PAIR (a) — with row 3, separates a pure ratio from anything carrying an additive term

SAME-RATIO PAIR (b) — identical 1:2 at near-double magnitude. Equal readouts = pure ratio; different = additive terms are real. 40/80 was the original plan and is unreachable: the bar slider maxes at 65
FREE ROW — the game's default bars. Not one of the three settings and NOT FITTED TO ANYTHING, which makes it the out-of-sample check. It earned its keep: see theRowThatKilledTheTidyAnswer

structureHolds: THE SOLVED FORM SURVIVES ON A SECOND CAR. All three structural predictions
made before the data was taken came true:
1. EQUAL BARS DO NOT READ 0.500. 30/30 gives 0.49. The per-axle terms are
2. THE SAME-RATIO PAIR SPLITS. 20/40 reads 0.51 and 32.5/65 reads 0.52 —
identical 1:2 ratios at near-double magnitude giving different answers,
which is only possible with an additive term. Every pure-ratio candidate
model (M1, M3) is dead here exactly as it was on the GR86.
3. THE DIRECTION IS RIGHT. This car carries a stiffer front at both bar and
spring and reads BELOW 0.5, which is what a REAR-share model requires.
So MB = R/(F+R) with F = arF + (spring term) + tF and R likewise. The form
generalises, as roll stiffness should. Only the numbers are the car's.
solve: Springs are held on all four rows, so the spring term and the axle constant
cannot be separated here — they lump into one per-axle constant each:
F = arF + A        R = arR + B        MB = R / (F + R)
Rows 1 and 2 both total 60 points of bar, so they share a denominator and
the algebra is trivial: 10/S = 0.51 - 0.49 = 0.02, giving S = 500, A = 225,
B = 215. That is the tidy answer AND IT IS WRONG — see below.
Done honestly, by taking every (A, B) that reproduces all four printed
readouts, the consistent region is a narrow diagonal band:
THE SCALE IS LOOSE AND THE SHARE IS PINNED, which is exactly what a ratio
readout can and cannot tell you. Anything quoting A and B as single numbers
from this data is quoting noise; the front share is the measurement.
Compare the GR86 at its own sweep springs: A = 120.7, B = 128.5, front
share 0.484 on a car that is 54% front. The Civic is 0.517 at 57% front.
Both sit about 5.5 points BELOW the car's front weight distribution, which
is a two-point pattern and nothing more — but it is the first hint that the
per-axle terms are predictable rather than merely measurable. A third car
either kills it or makes it a formula.
theRowThatKilledTheTidyAnswer: Row 0 was free — the default bars, read before any of this started, fitted
to nothing. It is the reason the tidy solve did not ship.
A = 225, B = 215 reproduces rows 1, 2 and 3 exactly.
On row 0 it predicts 0.4803, which prints 0.48. Measured: 0.47.
Rows 1 and 2 are two equations in two unknowns, so they CANNOT fail — any
solve fits them by construction, and row 3 agreeing looks like
confirmation. The only row capable of falsifying anything was the one
This is the third time in two days the tidier answer has been the wrong
one. The habit that catches it is cheap: take one reading you have no
intention of fitting, and check it last.
barsMoveBraking: UNASKED-FOR, AND OBJECTIVE. Anti-roll bars move the Performance panel's
braking distances while leaving everything else alone:
1.1 ft across 60-0, about 1.5%, on a panel that repeats to 0.1 ft. Real,
not noise. Note rows 1 and 2 carry the SAME total bar (60) and still differ
by 0.4 ft, so it is not simply total roll stiffness — distribution matters.
Four points is not a model and no conclusion is drawn here. What it does
mean is that S4, brake balance versus stopping distance, has an anti-roll
confound that has to be held, and that bars have an objective handle on
Lateral G was 1.20/1.36 on all four rows and 0-60, 0-100 and top speed did
not move at all. S5 keeps its provisional 'no'.

sliderRange._note: Case R1, free with the extremes: the front spring slider on this car runs 310.7 to 1553.7 lb/in, a 5.0x span. Nobody had ever recorded a real range before.

theLinearSpringTermIsFALSIFIED: *** THIS OVERTURNS THE SHAPE OF THE SOLVED MODEL. READ BEFORE USING IT. ***
The wide sweep was taken to narrow the exchange rate. It did something more
useful: it killed the term it was measuring.
At bars held 30/30 with the rear spring fixed, the model MB = R/(F+R) with
F = arF + ws*spF + tF requires (1-MB)/MB to be a STRAIGHT LINE in spF. That
test needs no knowledge of ws, tF or tR. It fails:
spF      MB     (1-MB)/MB    slope to the next point
The slope varies by more than 2x, and NO straight line fits inside all five
rounding windows — not even dropping the 1553.7 row. The curve is concave:
the spring's influence per lb/in falls off as the spring gets stiffer.
WHAT DOES FIT. Testing (1-MB)/MB linear in spF^p, the feasible exponents
are p in [0.45, 0.61]. p = 1 is excluded outright. p = 0.5 is allowed and
p = 2/3 is not.
p = 0.5 has an obvious physical reading and it is worth naming as a
HYPOTHESIS, not a finding: suspension frequency goes as sqrt(k/m), so a
square-root spring term is what you get if the game builds this readout
from FREQUENCIES rather than from rates. That would also explain why the
app's own spring model is a frequency-vs-PI curve. It is one car, five
rounded points, and the bar term has not been tested the same way — the
bars entered linearly over 20 to 65 and nobody has checked whether they
too are sub-linear over a wider span.
WHY THIS WAS NOT CAUGHT BEFORE, WHICH IS THE REAL LESSON:
GR86  fitted over spring 328.1 .. 608.1     1.85x span
Civic six-row set that fit    492 .. 914    1.86x span
Civic with the extremes     310.7 .. 1553.7  5.00x span
Both earlier solves lived inside a 1.9x window, and over 1.9x a concave
curve is indistinguishable from a line at two-decimal resolution. Re-run on
the GR86's own rows, EVERY exponent from 0.3 to 1.0 fits — its data cannot
discriminate at all. So the linear model was never confirmed; it was never
stressed.
The GR86 solve is not wrong. It is a LOCAL LINEARISATION that is accurate
near the tune it was measured at and drifts away from it. Tier 0 in
CLAUDE.md has to say so.
whichVindicatesTheAppsGUIDANCE: An accident worth noticing. C4 replaced the app's fixed '+/-0.5 ARB per 1%'
rule with a two-reading calibration: read MB, add 10 to the rear bar, read
again, scale. That was chosen because the COEFFICIENTS are per-car.
It turns out to be the right answer for a better reason than the one it was
chosen for. Measuring the local slope is exactly what you do with a
function that is curved rather than linear — it recalibrates at the tune
you are actually sitting at, which a global constant cannot do however well
it is measured. Had C4 shipped a per-car sensitivity NUMBER instead, this
sweep would have just invalidated it.
exchangeRateNotSettled: M9 ASKED WHETHER THE SPRING-TO-BAR EXCHANGE RATE IS A GAME CONSTANT.
THE ANSWER IS 'CONSISTENT WITH IT, BUT NOT SHOWN' — AND THAT IS THE
ANSWER, NOT A FAILURE TO GET ONE.
All six Civic rows solved together with ws, tF and tR all free:
ws  in [0.104, 0.152]        GR86 measured 0.150
0.150 is inside, near the top edge. So the data cannot reject the
hypothesis and cannot confirm it either: the band is +/-20% wide because
MB prints to two decimals and a +/-30% spring lever only moves it three
printing steps.
Holding ws at exactly 0.150, the axle constants land at:
Roughly double the GR86's, on a car 571 lb heavier — and NEARLY EQUAL to
each other, where the GR86's were clearly rear-biased. Those numbers are
conditional on ws=0.150 and move if it is not; quoted to show the shape,
not as a measurement.
WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the same two rows at the spring slider's actual
MINIMUM and MAXIMUM rather than +/-30%. The screenshots show plenty of
travel left at both ends. A wider lever is the only thing that narrows a
band set by rounding — more rows at the same spread will not.
theFalseRejectionIAlmostPublished: RECORDED BECAUSE THE NEAR-MISS IS THE LESSON, AND IT IS A NEW FAILURE MODE
FOR THIS REPO — not a rounded readout this time, but a coarse search grid.
The first solve stepped tF and tR by 1 and reported ws in [0.106, 0.148],
excluding 0.150, and the write-up 'the exchange rate does NOT transfer'
was one keystroke from being committed.
It was a grid artifact. Re-run with tR solved as an exact interval instead
of sampled, ws=0.150 fits all six rows comfortably, with tF in a 7-point
window the integer grid stepped straight over.
The tell was there and was nearly ignored: an exclusion whose boundary
(0.148) sits 1.3% from the value being excluded is not an exclusion, it is
a resolution limit. Any bound that lands that close to the number in
question is a prompt to re-derive it a different way before believing it.
springsMoveBrakingToo: Front spring rate, bars held at 30/30, everything else baseline:
2.9% across 60-0, which dwarfs the 1.5% the bars produced. But it is NOT
monotonic — the baseline 703 is the worst of the three, with both softer
and stiffer braking shorter. Three points cannot tell a real optimum from
a misreading, and nothing is concluded here.
It does mean S4 has a second confound: brake distance responds to springs
AND bars, so a brake sweep has to hold both.
Top speed moved with the spring again (166.3 vs 166.5), which is the same
contradiction of the Top Speed claim seen on the GR86 and is still
incidental rather than controlled. S1 remains the case that settles it.
Lateral G was 1.20/1.36 on all six rows of this car. S5's 'no' now rests
on bar changes, spring changes, pressure, gearing and aero across two cars.

_note: Case P4, and it arrived from an unexpected direction: the UPGRADE screen
shows every readout for the installed part and the alternative side by
side. That is a controlled A/B with no tune drift between the two halves,
which is better than installing and re-reading could ever be.
CAVEAT ON THE ABSOLUTE VALUES: the Mechanical Balance shown here (0.44 /
0.46) matches neither the default-tune reading (0.47) nor the 30/30 bar
reading (0.49) taken in the tuning menu. The preview is evidently
computed at some tune state of its own. THE DELTA IS THE MEASUREMENT;
the absolute figures are not comparable to tuning-menu readings until
somebody establishes what tune the preview assumes.
whatItBuys: weight, front %, power, torque   ALL UNCHANGED
lateral G at 60 and 120          UNCHANGED at 1.20 / 1.36
So the app is right that width does not touch the stat block, and right
that it is not a grip upgrade in the lateral-G sense. It is wrong that
width changes nothing but brake bias: a point of PI buying 1.4% of
braking and two frames of 0-100 is a straightforwardly good trade, and
the build plan says nothing about it.
andMBWENTTHEWRONGWAY: PREDICTED: roll stiffness goes as the SQUARE of track, so a wider front
should stiffen the front, raise F, and LOWER MB (the rear share).
MEASURED: MB went UP, 0.44 -> 0.46. A wider front axle behaves like a
That is not a small discrepancy, it is the wrong sign, and it points at
what the readout actually is. Lateral load transfer at an axle goes as
roll stiffness DIVIDED BY track, not multiplied by it — so widening the
front reduces the front's share of load transfer and raises the rear's.
HYPOTHESIS: Mech. Balance is the rear axle's share of lateral LOAD
TRANSFER, not of roll stiffness. At fixed geometry the two differ only
by a constant, which is exactly why every bar and spring row fitted
THE DISCRIMINATOR IS REAR TRACK WIDTH, and it is one screenshot:
load-transfer reading (track divides)  ->  wider REAR LOWERS MB
roll-stiffness reading (track squared) ->  wider REAR RAISES MB
Front already went up, so the load-transfer reading predicts DOWN. If it
goes up instead, both readings are wrong and the term is something else.

whatIsStillLumped: A and B each contain a spring term plus an axle constant, and bar-only rows
cannot separate them. Two more readings would:
That gives this car's spring-to-bar exchange rate. The GR86's was 0.150 of
a bar point per lb/in, i.e. one bar point per 6.7 lb/in. IF THAT NUMBER
TRANSFERS it is a game constant rather than a car constant, and the whole
model collapses to two per-car unknowns instead of three — which would make
a two-reading calibration exact rather than approximate.
Sanity check that it is at least possible: assuming 0.150 holds, the spring
terms here are 105.5 front and 89.5 rear, leaving tF in [62.0, 114.5] and
tR in [66.5, 116.0]. Both positive and both larger than the GR86's 50.5 and
72.3 on a car 571 lb heavier. Nothing absurd, so the hypothesis survives to
method: One variable per row: bars only. Springs, ride heights and pressures are
copied into every row above from defaultTune and must not move — they are
in the model, and a drift in any of them gets blamed on the bars.
Nothing recorded while the panel reads SIMULATING. That cost two rows the
